projects.title: Chess Club
projects.description: A full-stack chess application built as a complete, self-hosted product: you play against Stockfish at several difficulty levels, your games and stats are tracked over time, and an estimated ELO reflects your progression. A Rust backend (Axum, async-graphql, SQLx on SQLite) exposes a GraphQL API, and a SvelteKit frontend served by Nginx consumes it. The whole stack runs in Docker Compose.
highlights: Built the full game loop in Rust: game creation, move validation, timers, results and persistence in SQLite
Integrated Stockfish over UCI, tuning skill level, think time and deliberate imperfections per difficulty
Tracked user profiles, per-level statistics, win streaks, play time and a leaderboard, with an estimated ELO derived from results
Shipped it self-hosted: Docker Compose stack, SQLite volume, Nginx frontend and an automated GitHub Actions deploy to my home server over WireGuard

steps.label: LAYER 01 / 04 · SVELTE + RUST
steps.text: A Svelte interface with a responsive board, promotion dialog and timers, backed by a Rust server. I chose this pair on purpose to keep the architecture as light as possible in RAM and CPU: Svelte compiles to plain JavaScript with no heavy runtime, and Rust gives a small, predictable memory footprint. Static assets are served by Nginx.

steps.label: LAYER 02 / 04 · API
steps.text: A GraphQL API (async-graphql) exposing createUser, createGame, makeMove, getUserProfile and getLeaderboard. Each resolver delegates to the game and stats services, which handle move legality, streaks and per-level statistics.

steps.label: LAYER 03 / 04 · ENGINE
steps.text: Stockfish is driven over UCI. Difficulty maps to skill level, think time and deliberate imperfection, so weaker levels make realistic mistakes.

steps.label: LAYER 04 / 04 · SELF-HOSTED
steps.text: I wanted a full self-hosted project: no managed cloud services, just containers on my own server. Docker Compose runs the backend, the frontend and the SQLite volume, and GitHub Actions deploys over WireGuard. I owned every layer, from the engine to the deployment.

projects.title: MetaCulture — XRPL NFT Experience
projects.description: A proof of concept built during the XRPL Commons hackathon (3 to 5 May) for an art exhibition at the Centre Pompidou. The goal was to teach an AI the artist's data so it could take the artist's place and let visitors talk with it about the works. Access to the AI is gated by an NFT used as an access token, with an alternative for visitors without a crypto wallet: they can sign in with a simple email address.
highlights: Gated access to the AI experience with an NFT on the XRPL, used as a digital access token
Built a fallback login with email for visitors who do not have a digital wallet, so the experience stays accessible
Trained an AI on the artist's data so it could speak in the artist's place and guide visitors through the works in conversation
Connected the XRPL, Xaman wallet, Pinata, Brevo (transactional email) and Predibase (AI platform) in one Docker Compose stack
Worked in a four-person team during the hackathon, with a Make-driven build and run workflow

steps.label: VIEW 01 / 03 · NFT ACCESS
steps.text: An NFT on the XRPL acts as the access token to the AI experience, with wallet sign-in through Xaman. Visitors without a wallet can instead sign in with an email address, which keeps the exhibition open to everyone.

steps.label: VIEW 02 / 03 · AI GUIDE
steps.text: An AI model trained on the artist's own data, served through Predibase, takes the artist's place in the exhibition: visitors ask questions and explore the works in conversation, as if the artist were guiding them.

steps.label: VIEW 03 / 03 · EXHIBITION
steps.text: The whole PoC runs as a Docker Compose stack, built and started with Make, so it can be deployed quickly for an exhibition. It explores how creative technology can make blockchain access feel simple for visitors.

projects.title: Aléas — Randomized Theatre Experience
projects.description: An improvised theatre show where the actors hand their fate to chance: staging, sound, light and timing are all controlled at random by a computer, and the performers have to adapt live. It was built to experiment with randomness in improvised theatre and to bridge theatre and the science of chance. I worked on the system that generates these random scenes, music and light sequences, while keeping enough structure that the show still holds together on stage.
highlights: Built the random generation logic for scenes, music and light cues, with weighted templates and random durations and fades
Made the lighting feel coherent despite randomness: light scenes chase across the fixtures in sequences with timed fades, so even chance-driven changes read as intentional
Scheduled background music at random intervals and tracks, so the performers have to react to sound they cannot anticipate
Applied creative programming to a live show presented at the Avignon Festival

steps.label: PART 01 / 03 · RANDOM SEED
steps.text: The computer draws the shape of each performance: random durations for each scene, random fades and random scene choices, so no two shows follow the same structure. The performers have to adapt to whatever comes next.

steps.label: PART 02 / 03 · LIGHT & SOUND
steps.text: Music appears intermittently, at random times and from random tracks, so it can cut into a scene without warning. In the meantime the lights keep a coherent pattern: during a moment of intensity, the light scenes chase across the fixtures in timed sequences, with smooth fades that keep the stage readable even when the cues are random.

steps.label: PART 03 / 03 · SCENE STATES
steps.text: The lights are driven over DMX512 from a generated show file, so the random scene states run live on the stage. The performers improvise against a stage that is random but never incoherent, which is what gives the piece its tension.

projects.title: Defense Hackathon — Drone Detection
projects.description: A defense hackathon project held in Paris (7 to 9 November 2025) on the Synteza-1 challenge: detecting and tracking small FPV drones with cameras and AI, in real time, at about 500 metres and without human intervention. The project covers a full pipeline, from dataset preparation to a YOLO detection model, and a Next.js monitoring dashboard that places each detection on a map and raises danger alerts.
highlights: Built a YOLOv8s detection pipeline for a single 'Drone' class, fine-tuned from pretrained weights on a labelled dataset of about 2,500 positive and 1,000 negative images
Prepared the data with a reproducible 70/20/10 train/val/test split (fixed seed) and augmented the training set with flips, rotations, scaling, perspective, blur, noise and brightness changes

Configured training through environment variables (device auto-detection GPU/CPU, mixed precision, disk cache, early stopping, checkpoints), with the Makefile driving split, augmentation, training and prediction
Created a Next.js dashboard that polls the latest detections, shows annotated frames and estimates each drone's position from the camera and bounding box, with danger alerts and browser notifications
Delivered the full pipeline end to end within the hackathon sprint, aiming at the challenge target of 50% detection accuracy

steps.label: TRACK 01 / 03 · DETECTION
steps.text: A YOLOv8s model fine-tuned to detect drones in camera frames. The dataset is split 70/20/10 with a fixed seed, and the training set is augmented with flips, rotations, scaling, perspective, blur, noise and brightness changes so the model copes with real-world variation.

steps.label: TRACK 02 / 03 · DASHBOARD
steps.text: A Next.js dashboard receives each detection from the Python pipeline, shows the annotated frame and estimates the drone's position on a map from the camera location and bounding box, with a bearing toward the observer. Danger alerts appear in the interface and as browser notifications.

steps.label: TRACK 03 / 03 · SPRINT
steps.text: Built within a single hackathon sprint on the Synteza-1 challenge: a pipeline from dataset to live monitoring, reproducible through a Makefile, with a clear path to a more robust, real-time system.
